questionText: A small unmanned aircraft's manufacturer publishes no maintenance schedule. What is the operator expected to do?
answers: Establish a reasonable maintenance schedule of their own
Perform no scheduled maintenance, since none is specified
Return the aircraft to the manufacturer every 12 calendar months
Apply the maintenance schedule from 14 CFR part 43
correctAnswer: Establish a reasonable maintenance schedule of their own
hint: The absence of manufacturer instructions moves the responsibility rather than removing it.

prompt:
AC 107-2A, Maintenance: Unscheduled maintenance is prompted by an event or a discovery rather than by an interval. A hard landing, a strike, an overheated battery, or an abnormal indication in flight are all reasons to inspect the aircraft before it is flown again.

Source: https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf
questionText: A small unmanned aircraft makes a hard landing but appears undamaged. What does this call for?
answers: Unscheduled maintenance: an inspection before the next flight
Nothing, provided no damage is visible from a distance
A report to the FAA within 10 calendar days
Replacement of the airframe regardless of its condition
correctAnswer: Unscheduled maintenance: an inspection before the next flight
hint: The event itself, not visible damage, is what triggers this category of maintenance.

prompt:
14 CFR 107.15: No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft system unless it is in a condition for safe operation. Before each flight, the remote pilot in command must check the small unmanned aircraft system to determine that it is in a condition for safe operation, and must discontinue the flight if an unsafe condition develops.

Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-107.15
questionText: Under 14 CFR 107.15, what must the remote pilot in command do if an unsafe condition develops during flight?
answers: Discontinue the flight
Continue to the planned landing point regardless
Land only if the condition affects the control link
Complete the flight and note the condition in the maintenance record
correctAnswer: Discontinue the flight
hint: 107.15 covers both the preflight check and what happens when the condition changes in the air.

prompt:
AC 107-2A, Maintenance Recordkeeping: Although part 107 prescribes no maintenance log format, keeping a record of what was done, when, and by whom lets an operator establish trends, show that scheduled work was performed, and hand an aircraft to another pilot with its history intact.

Source: https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf
questionText: Why is a maintenance record recommended even though part 107 does not prescribe one?
answers: It establishes what was done and when, so trends and completed work can be verified
It is required before an aircraft may be registered under part 48
It substitutes for the preflight inspection required by 107.49
It is required by Air Traffic Control before airspace authorization is granted
correctAnswer: It establishes what was done and when, so trends and completed work can be verified
hint: The value is evidentiary: knowing the aircraft's history rather than guessing at it.

prompt:
AC 107-2A, Maintenance: Propellers are among the most frequently damaged components on a small unmanned aircraft. Cracks, nicks, chips, and deformation unbalance the propeller, increase vibration, and can lead to failure in flight. A damaged propeller is replaced rather than repaired.

Source: https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf
questionText: A preflight inspection reveals a small crack in one propeller blade. What is the appropriate action?
answers: Replace the propeller before flight
File the crack smooth and continue with the flight
Fly with reduced payload to lower the load on the blade
Balance the crack by making a matching cut on the opposite blade
correctAnswer: Replace the propeller before flight
hint: Propellers are replaced, not repaired, and vibration from an unbalanced blade compounds quickly.

prompt:
AC 107-2A paragraph 7.2 directs operators to maintain the small UAS and its components in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions, and Appendix B.5 notes that lithium-based battery fires can be caused by improper charging, extreme temperatures, damage, or mishandling. Manufacturers accordingly specify a storage charge level and a storage temperature range.

Source: https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf
questionText: Which two factors do manufacturers typically specify for storing lithium batteries?
answers: State of charge and temperature range
Altitude and humidity
Cycle count and cell chemistry
Discharge rate and propeller pitch
correctAnswer: State of charge and temperature range
hint: Both concern the conditions the battery sits in between flights.

prompt:
AC 107-2A paragraph 7.2 includes system software upgrades in the definition of small UAS maintenance, and 7.2.2 states that where an unscheduled software update is required to correct a problem, flight operations should not occur until the issue is corrected. Firmware can change failsafe and return-to-home behaviour, so an update is applied on the ground with time to verify the result.

Source: https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf
questionText: When should a firmware update be applied to a small unmanned aircraft system?
answers: On the ground with time to verify the aircraft afterwards, not immediately before a flight
Immediately before every flight, so the aircraft is always current
Only after an accident has been reported to the FAA
In flight, so any problem can be observed directly
correctAnswer: On the ground with time to verify the aircraft afterwards, not immediately before a flight
hint: An update can change failsafe behaviour, so the verification has to happen before the aircraft is needed.

prompt:
AC 107-2A, Maintenance: Some repairs are beyond what an operator should attempt. When a component's condition is in doubt, or a repair calls for tools, parts, or knowledge the operator does not have, the manufacturer or a qualified technician should perform the work.

Source: https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf
questionText: A remote pilot is unsure whether an airframe arm was damaged in a collision. What is the appropriate course of action?
answers: Have the manufacturer or a qualified technician assess it before further flight
Fly a short test flight at low altitude to see whether it holds
Continue flying and monitor for vibration
Replace the propellers, since arm damage always originates there
correctAnswer: Have the manufacturer or a qualified technician assess it before further flight
hint: Doubt about a structural component is resolved on the ground by someone qualified, not in the air.

prompt:
AC 107-2A paragraph 7.2 directs operators to follow the manufacturer's instructions. Compass and inertial sensor calibration reads the earth's magnetic field, so manufacturers direct that it be performed away from ferrous metal — structures, vehicles, and reinforced concrete.

Source: https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf
questionText: Where should a compass calibration be performed?
answers: Away from metal structures, vehicles, and reinforced concrete
Directly beside the transport vehicle, for convenience
Indoors, where wind will not disturb the aircraft
On a metal surface, to provide a consistent magnetic reference
correctAnswer: Away from metal structures, vehicles, and reinforced concrete
hint: The instrument is reading the earth's magnetic field, so anything ferrous nearby corrupts it.

prompt:
14 CFR 107.49: Before flight, the remote pilot in command must assess the operating environment, check local weather and airspace, inspect the small unmanned aircraft system to ensure all systems are functioning properly, verify that sufficient power exists to operate for the intended time, and ensure any object attached or carried is secure.

Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-107.49
questionText: Which of the following is part of the preflight action required by 14 CFR 107.49?
answers: Verifying that sufficient power exists to operate for the intended flight time
Filing a flight plan with the nearest Flight Service Station
Recording the flight in a logbook retained for 24 calendar months
Obtaining a maintenance release signed by a certificated mechanic
correctAnswer: Verifying that sufficient power exists to operate for the intended flight time
hint: 107.49 lists environment, weather and airspace, systems, power, and secured objects.

prompt:
14 CFR 107.29: No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft system at night unless the aircraft has lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles, with a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision. The remote pilot in command may reduce the intensity of, but may not extinguish, the lighting if doing so is in the interest of safety.

Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-107.29
questionText: What anti-collision lighting does 14 CFR 107.29 require for night operations?
answers: Lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles with a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision
Steady white lighting visible for at least 1 statute mile
Lighting visible for at least 5 statute miles in all directions
No lighting, provided a visual observer is used
correctAnswer: Lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles with a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision
hint: The distance matches the minimum flight visibility required by 107.51.

prompt:
14 CFR 107.29(b) and (c): The anti-collision lighting requirement applies both at night and during periods of civil twilight. For the purposes of this section, civil twilight means — except in Alaska — the period beginning 30 minutes before official sunrise and ending at official sunrise, and the period beginning at official sunset and ending 30 minutes after official sunset. In Alaska it is the period of civil twilight defined in the Air Almanac.

Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-107.29
questionText: Is anti-collision lighting required during civil twilight?
answers: Yes, the same lighting required at night applies during civil twilight
No, lighting is required only after the end of evening civil twilight
Only if the operation is conducted in controlled airspace
Only if the operation is conducted over people
correctAnswer: Yes, the same lighting required at night applies during civil twilight
hint: 107.29 addresses both night and civil twilight in the same requirement.

prompt:
14 CFR 1.1: Night is defined as the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight, as published in the Air Almanac and converted to local time.

Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-1.1
questionText: How is night defined for the purposes of the regulations?
answers: The period between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight
The period between sunset and sunrise
The period beginning 30 minutes after sunset and ending 30 minutes before sunrise
Any period when the ground is not illuminated by natural light
correctAnswer: The period between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight
hint: The definition is anchored to civil twilight, not to sunset and sunrise themselves.

prompt:
14 CFR 107.29: The remote pilot in command may reduce the intensity of the anti-collision lighting when doing so is in the interest of safety, but the lighting may not be turned off entirely while the aircraft is operated at night or during civil twilight.

Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-107.29
questionText: May a remote pilot dim the anti-collision lighting during a night operation?
answers: Yes, the intensity may be reduced in the interest of safety, but the lighting may not be extinguished
No, the lighting must remain at full intensity at all times
Yes, and it may be extinguished entirely if it interferes with the camera
Only with a certificate of waiver issued under 107.200
correctAnswer: Yes, the intensity may be reduced in the interest of safety, but the lighting may not be extinguished
hint: The rule permits one of dimming and switching off, and forbids the other.

prompt:
14 CFR 107.65 and the 2021 amendment to part 107: Night operations no longer require a certificate of waiver. A remote pilot may operate at night provided the aircraft carries the anti-collision lighting required by 107.29 and the pilot has completed the initial or recurrent training that covers night operations.

Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-107.29
questionText: What does a remote pilot need in order to operate at night under the current rule?
answers: The anti-collision lighting required by 107.29 and current training covering night operations
A certificate of waiver issued under 107.200 for every night flight
A visual observer stationed at the aircraft's maximum range
Prior authorization from Air Traffic Control regardless of airspace class
correctAnswer: The anti-collision lighting required by 107.29 and current training covering night operations
hint: The waiver requirement was replaced by a lighting requirement and a training requirement.

prompt:
AC 107-2A, Night Operations: Depth perception and the ability to judge distance are substantially degraded in darkness, which makes it harder to tell how far away the aircraft is and how far it has drifted. Surveying the site in daylight beforehand gives the pilot a mental picture of the obstacles that will not be visible at night.

Source: https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/19_phak_ch17.pdf
questionText: Why is a daylight survey of the operating site recommended before a night operation?
answers: Obstacles that will be invisible at night can be identified and their positions memorized
Airspace authorization is only issued during daylight hours
Anti-collision lighting cannot be tested after dark
The preflight inspection required by 107.49 may not be performed at night
correctAnswer: Obstacles that will be invisible at night can be identified and their positions memorized
hint: What changes after dark is what the pilot can see, not what the rules allow.

prompt:
14 CFR 107.31 and AC 107-2A: The visual line of sight requirement does not change at night. The remote pilot must still be able to see the unmanned aircraft throughout the flight with vision unaided by any device other than corrective lenses, which in practice means the anti-collision lighting has to be adequate for the pilot to keep the aircraft in sight.

Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-107.31
questionText: How does the visual line of sight requirement of 107.31 apply at night?
answers: It applies unchanged, so the aircraft's lighting must let the pilot keep it in sight
It is suspended at night in favour of the lighting requirement in 107.29
It is satisfied by watching the aircraft's position on the control station display
It applies only within 400 feet of the control station at night
correctAnswer: It applies unchanged, so the aircraft's lighting must let the pilot keep it in sight
hint: 107.29 adds a requirement for night; it does not remove any of the daytime ones.

prompt:
AC 107-2A paragraph 7.2 directs operators to maintain the small UAS in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions. At night an aircraft's orientation is far harder to judge, because the airframe itself is not visible and only its lights are, so many manufacturers fit different coloured lights front and rear to show which way the aircraft is facing.

Source: https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf
questionText: Why do many small unmanned aircraft use different coloured lights at the front and rear?
answers: So the remote pilot can determine the aircraft's orientation when the airframe is not visible
To satisfy the 3 statute mile visibility requirement of 107.29
To identify the aircraft's registration number from the ground
To signal the aircraft's remaining battery state to observers
correctAnswer: So the remote pilot can determine the aircraft's orientation when the airframe is not visible
hint: The problem the colours solve is knowing which way the aircraft is pointing.

prompt:
AC 107-2A, Night Operations: Exposure to a bright light source destroys dark adaptation that took roughly 30 minutes to build. Vehicle headlights, phone screens at full brightness, and work lights at the control station all cost the pilot night vision that then has to be regained.

Source: https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/19_phak_ch17.pdf
questionText: A remote pilot checks a phone at full screen brightness midway through a night operation. What is the consequence?
answers: Dark adaptation is lost and must be regained over roughly 30 minutes
Dark adaptation is unaffected, since the screen is not a flashing light
The aircraft's anti-collision lighting becomes harder for other pilots to see
Depth perception improves because the eyes have a nearby reference
correctAnswer: Dark adaptation is lost and must be regained over roughly 30 minutes
hint: Dark adaptation is slow to gain and immediate to lose.

prompt:
AC 107-2A, Night Operations: Judging the distance and altitude of another aircraft at night is considerably harder, because only its lights are visible and there is no size cue to fix the distance. Manned aircraft position lights — red on the left wingtip, green on the right, white at the tail — are the main indication of another aircraft's direction of travel.

Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-25.1385
questionText: A remote pilot at night sees a green light on the right and a red light on the left of an approaching aircraft. What does this indicate?
answers: The aircraft is heading toward the observer
The aircraft is heading away from the observer
The aircraft is crossing from left to right
The aircraft is stationary, such as a helicopter in a hover
correctAnswer: The aircraft is heading toward the observer
hint: Red marks the aircraft's left wingtip and green its right; work out where the observer must be standing to see them that way round.
